key_finding: Across six agents on BrowseComp-Plus and BrowseComp, answer accuracy tracks cumulative retrieval recall far more than the number of searches or context consumed, and the best agents issue far fewer redundant queries while useful evidence often surfaces early yet agents keep searching anyway.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis using human-annotated document relevance judgments, holding the retrieval model and evaluation harness fixed across six long-horizon search agents on BrowseComp-Plus, validated on BrowseComp with an open-web API.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the premise that more agentic search effort produces better answers and finds it weakly supported, redirecting where the project should look for gains — evidence quality and stopping criteria, not search volume — and gives a concrete decomposition (retrieval gap vs. utilization gap) to measure by.
limitations: relies on human-annotated relevance judgments that may not generalize to other corpora
only six agents studied, all on two closely related benchmarks
relevance_reason: A trajectory-level diagnostic that separates what specific agentic moves (reformulation, stopping) actually contribute, directly answering brief questions 2 and 4.

key_finding: PaSa-7B, an RL-trained autonomous paper-search agent, surpasses the best Google-based baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on the real-world RealScholarQuery benchmark.
methodology: RL-optimized LLM agent trained on a synthetic 35k-query dataset (AutoScholarQuery), evaluated against Google, Google Scholar, ChatGPT, and GPT-o1 baselines on a newly built real-world benchmark (RealScholarQuery).
why_it_matters: Provides a concrete, numeric anchor for how large an agentic gain over single-query search-engine baselines can be, and its two-benchmark construction (synthetic training set vs. real evaluation set) is exactly the kind of contamination-control design decision question 3 asks about.
limitations: trained on synthetic queries which may not fully represent real research needs despite the separate real benchmark
comparison baselines are general web search engines rather than academic search APIs specifically tuned for recall
relevance_reason: A flagship agentic paper-search system with an explicit baseline comparison and benchmark construction, central to the brief's core question.

key_finding: A bounded citation-graph exploration agent (Crase) that expands seed papers along a 1.5-hop citation neighborhood and prunes unsupported edges outperforms open-ended deep research agents built on proprietary models by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch and a further benchmark.
methodology: Single seed search plus fixed-depth citation-graph expansion, entailment-based edge pruning, and recency-aware random-walk ranking over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus, compared against deep research agents.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal as the specific mechanism carrying the gain over open-ended agentic search, with an explicit cost/recall tradeoff — exactly the kind of mechanism attribution the brief's decision 2 needs.
limitations: evaluated on a fixed 500K-paper arXiv corpus, not the full scholarly literature
bounded 1.5-hop design may miss papers outside citation neighborhoods of seeds
relevance_reason: Directly attributes a measured recall gain to citation-graph traversal versus open-ended agentic search, the sharpest mechanism-level evidence in the set.

key_finding: In a controlled comparison across eight expert research projects, the overlap between human- and AI-selected references was under 6%, and 64% of AI-generated references from mid-2025 LLMs had at least one incorrect metadata field despite only 3% being outright fabrications.
methodology: Controlled parallel literature-review study: human experts and AI systems (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini, and later ChatGPT Pro 5.5) independently perform identical literature-search tasks across eight physics/astrophysics/cosmology projects.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the brief's premise that agentic literature-search gains are real: even sophisticated deep-research LLM tools barely overlap with expert-selected references and carry a high metadata-error rate, which should temper how much weight the scan gives to self-reported agent recall numbers.
limitations: small sample of eight projects
domain-specific to physics/astrophysics/cosmology, which may not generalize to other scientific fields
does not test purpose-built agentic literature-search systems, only general-purpose assistants
relevance_reason: The starkest evidence in the shortlist that agentic/LLM-assisted literature search underperforms expert human search, answering the brief's decision 4 head-on.

key_finding: WisPaper's Deep Search module achieves 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, with the validation model reaching 93.70% accuracy at filtering hallucinated candidates.
methodology: End-to-end agent system combining keyword retrieval, agentic deep-search validation, and a user-profile-driven recommendation loop, evaluated on TaxoBench against an O3 baseline.
why_it_matters: The reported gain over the baseline is modest (about 1.3 points of recall), which is useful counter-evidence to the premise that agentic systems produce large, robust improvements over single-query search.
limitations: gain over baseline is small and not tested for statistical significance
TaxoBench construction and contamination controls are not described in the abstract
relevance_reason: An end-to-end agentic literature-search system reporting a small, explicit recall gain over a non-agentic baseline, relevant to decisions 1 and 2.

key_finding: ReBOL, which uses LLM query reformulations to seed a Bayesian-optimization posterior over document relevance, achieves 46.5% vs 35.0% recall@100 against the best LLM reranker baseline on Robust04.
methodology: Bayesian optimization over multimodal relevance posteriors initialized by LLM query reformulations, with iterative batched LLM relevance scoring, evaluated on five BEIR datasets with two LLMs.
why_it_matters: A concrete retrieval/reranking mechanism combining reformulation with iterative relevance estimation that could underlie an agentic literature-search system's retrieval stage, though it is demonstrated on general IR benchmarks rather than scholarly search.
limitations: evaluated on general BEIR IR datasets, not scientific-literature-specific benchmarks
latency and cost tradeoffs against simpler rerankers are only partially explored
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking method combining query reformulation with iterative optimization, relevant to the brief's underlying-technique question, but demonstrated outside the scientific-literature-search setting so capped as off-domain.

key_finding: On a wiki-style corpus, removing followable cross-reference links roughly doubles the number of searches per grounded fact at scale, while some facts deemed unreachable by search alone were recovered via link traversal or read-derived re-querying.
methodology: Pre-registered two-arm controlled study on a generated corpus (50/500/5000 pages) with real vs. link-stripped cross-references, measuring grounded coverage, search cost, and fetch provenance across 99 episodes of a Claude agent.
why_it_matters: Provides a rigorously controlled quantification of how link/graph traversal reduces search cost for an agent, a mechanism directly analogous to citation-graph traversal in scholarly search, though demonstrated on an organizational wiki rather than a scientific corpus.
limitations: corpus is a synthetic organizational wiki, not a scientific literature corpus
unusual venue (Open MIND) and citation count inconsistent with a niche preprint, raising provenance questions
relevance_reason: Closely related evidence on how cross-reference/graph traversal reduces search cost for an LLM agent, but in a non-scientific-literature setting so capped as off-domain.

key_finding: LATTICE, an LLM-guided hierarchical search index with no embedding model in the retrieval loop, matches the best fine-tuned ensemble at 46.7 nDCG@10 on the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark and reaches 49.1 with a lightweight ensemble, while remaining competitive on NQ, SciFact, and SciDocs.
methodology: Top-down LLM-guided construction of a hierarchical document index from multi-level summaries, with calibrated path-aggregated LLM traversal at query time, benchmarked against embedding+LLM-verifier and sliding-window reranking baselines.
why_it_matters: Shows the standard cheap-embed-then-verify retrieval recipe fails on reasoning-intensive queries and that LLM-guided graph traversal can substitute for embedding retrieval entirely — directly informs which retrieval architecture choice underlies an agentic literature-search system's search stage.
limitations: evaluated primarily on BRIGHT and general IR benchmarks, not literature-search-specific benchmarks
token-budget tradeoffs favor reranking at low budgets, limiting when LATTICE's advantage applies
relevance_reason: A retrieval-architecture paper showing where embedding-based single-query retrieval fails and how hierarchical LLM-guided traversal fixes it, informing the retrieval/reranking layer under agentic search.

key_finding: On a fixed, human-verified corpus, Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86% accuracy while GPT-5 reaches 55.9%, rising to 70.1% with fewer search calls when paired with a Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever, showing the retriever choice alone drives large swings in deep-research performance.
methodology: A benchmark derived from BrowseComp with a fixed, curated document corpus, human-verified supporting documents, and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled disentanglement of retriever and agent contributions.
why_it_matters: Establishes exactly the kind of controlled baseline the brief's decision 1 needs — quantified retrieval-method ceilings (BM25 vs. dense) independent of agent capability — and is the benchmark other shortlisted papers (diagnostic and corpus-projection studies) build directly on.
limitations: corpus and negatives are mined from the benchmark's own queries, which the later ClimbMix-projection paper shows may inflate reported recall
single benchmark domain (BrowseComp-style complex web queries), not scholarly-paper search specifically
relevance_reason: The controlled benchmark underlying multiple other shortlisted papers' baseline and mechanism claims, central to how agentic gains in this literature are measured.

key_finding: Deep research agents exhibit an 'inertia bias' — becoming less objective when judging outcomes of their own prior queries/plans — and context isolation at webpage-triage and answer-validation decision points (NIS-Agent) reduces token cost by 33% while maintaining competitive performance across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark to isolate self-authored-action bias by controlling search observations, then evaluates a context-isolation intervention (NIS-Agent) across four deep-research benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Identifies a specific failure mode (self-judgment bias) internal to agentic search loops that could explain part of the gap between reported and actual gains, useful for the brief's question 4 on where gains fail to hold.
limitations: benchmarks (GAIA, WebWalkerQA) are general web-QA tasks rather than scientific-literature search specifically
improvement is measured mainly via cost reduction rather than large accuracy gains
relevance_reason: Names a specific mechanism-level failure mode in agentic search loops and a targeted fix, relevant to sequencing what to test and watch for in agent design.

key_finding: HySemRAG's structured field extraction achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001) than PDF-chunking approaches, with its agentic QA loop reaching 68.3% single-pass success and 99.0% citation accuracy.
methodology: Multi-stage ETL+RAG pipeline combining hybrid retrieval (semantic search, keyword filtering, knowledge-graph traversal), agentic self-correction, and post-hoc citation verification, evaluated across 643 observations from 60 testing sessions.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a concrete hybrid retrieval architecture (semantic + keyword + KG traversal) underlying automated literature synthesis with measured citation-accuracy and extraction-quality numbers, relevant to the retrieval/reranking layer the brief asks about.
limitations: single-author system paper with self-reported evaluation metrics
primary application domain (geospatial epidemiology) is outside the CS-venue evidence base the brief centers on
relevance_reason: A hybrid retrieval architecture (semantic, keyword, knowledge-graph) explicitly built for literature synthesis, directly matching the brief's retrieval-methods criterion.

key_finding: A systematic taxonomy of Deep Research agents finds that current benchmarks suffer from restricted external-knowledge access, sequential execution inefficiencies, and misalignment between evaluation metrics and agents' practical objectives.
methodology: Narrative survey and taxonomy construction covering information-acquisition strategies, tool-use frameworks, and planning/composition architectures across the Deep Research agent literature, with critical benchmark evaluation.
why_it_matters: Provides the field-level map and explicit critique of benchmark limitations that the brief's decision 3 needs to interpret any single system's reported numbers, and is the kind of synthesis paper other work in this scan argues with or extends.
limitations: narrative rather than systematic-protocol review, so coverage and inclusion criteria are not formally specified
no new empirical results of its own
relevance_reason: A survey/roadmap directly addressing benchmark construction limitations and taxonomizing agentic mechanisms, the synthesis the scan should ship alongside primary studies.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus's evidence into an independently-built 553M-document corpus (ClimbMix) causes the strongest agent's evidence recall to fall from 84.3% to 21.4% and answer accuracy to drop five points while issuing 63% more search calls.
methodology: A projection pipeline decomposes benchmark questions into atomic reasoning hops, re-grounds each hop in a corpus (ClimbMix) built without reference to the benchmark, and retains only questions verified by automatic checks, an independent agent, and human review; yields 57 fully re-grounded questions from 830 originals.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that a benchmark whose corpus was assembled per-query (BrowseComp-Plus) inflates reported retrieval performance relative to a more realistic, independently-built corpus — exactly the kind of gain-failure-under-a-different-corpus evidence the brief's decision 4 is looking for.
limitations: only 57 of 830 original questions survive the re-grounding pipeline, a large reduction in coverage
single projection target (ClimbMix); generality of the pipeline to other corpora is asserted but only one instance is shown
relevance_reason: The clearest demonstration in the shortlist that a widely-used agentic-search benchmark's reported gains do not survive a change of corpus, directly answering the brief's hardest question.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B, a multi-turn literature-search agent that frames search as executable workflow induction, raises Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over a base Qwen3.5-9B toolset agent, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Supervised workflow imitation plus preference optimization over controlled workflow corruptions; DAG-based executable search workflows combining keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, scoring, reranking, and evidence extraction, refined via multi-turn user feedback.
why_it_matters: Decomposes agentic literature search into explicit, editable operators (citation expansion, reranking, filtering) and shows the gain over an undifferentiated toolset baseline, directly informing which mechanisms carry the improvement rather than the system as a whole.
limitations: Baseline is a toolset agent, not single-query database search directly
Abstract gives no benchmark construction detail (query source, relevance labeling)
relevance_reason: Core system-design work matching the brief's interest in workflow-level attribution of agentic gains in literature search.

key_finding: EviReform's evidence-guided residual query reformulation for graph retrieval exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Separates retrieval-request revision from evidence aggregation in a graph; normalizes original and residual retrieval signals and propagates them between entity-sharing propositions; evaluated on standard multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a query-reformulation-plus-graph-propagation mechanism directly analogous to citation-graph traversal in literature-search agents, but tested only on generic multi-hop QA rather than scientific literature.
limitations: Evaluated on generic multi-hop QA datasets, not scientific literature search
No comparison to a single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: A closely related retrieval-reformulation technique for graph retrieval that could inform citation-graph traversal design, though off the literature-search setting.

key_finding: Coding 26 AI-scientist systems in full, the survey finds 83% of runnable systems release code but only 38% release seeds/execution traces and 38% report any novelty-verification method, with no LLM-era closed-loop system demonstrating an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Systematic survey screening 125 candidate works, coding 26 in full across seven audit dimensions (lifecycle stage, autonomy, evaluation method, artifacts, human-in-loop, novelty verification, result-selection disclosure).
why_it_matters: Documents a field-wide verification gap in AI-scientist systems that should temper how much we trust self-reported agentic gains generally, though it does not isolate literature-search benchmarks or mechanisms specifically.
limitations: Scope is the full research lifecycle, not literature search specifically
Abstract gives no detail on literature-search evaluation practices in particular
relevance_reason: A broader survey on verification of agentic research claims that indirectly supports the brief's skepticism toward unreplicated agentic gains.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves a 16.5x higher F1-score than Google Scholar and 37.8% higher F1-score than GPT-5.2 at about 1% of the cost across 38 disciplines (PaSaMaster-Bench), reducing source hallucination from 32.66% to zero.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving agentic retrieval combining iterative intent refinement, evidence-grounded ranking over verified papers (not generated citations), and planning-retrieval separation using frontier LLMs for intent and lightweight models for retrieval/scoring; evaluated on a new 38-discipline benchmark.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, quantified comparison against a single-query search baseline (Google Scholar) establishing how large the claimed agentic gain can be, directly bearing on decisions 1 and 2, though as an all-positive result it needs independent replication to test decision 4.
limitations: Self-reported new benchmark (PaSaMaster-Bench) not independently validated
No analysis of whether the reported gain holds under a different benchmark or metric
relevance_reason: Directly compares an agentic literature-retrieval system against a single-query database baseline and attributes gains to specific mechanisms, central to the brief's first two decisions.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature retrieval, summarization, and contradiction-detection tasks, identifying 2.34 ± 1.99 contradictions per paper with 70% human-validated.
methodology: Human-AI comparison methodology on real-world literature research tasks with unrestricted human comparators; introduces the LitQA2 benchmark that guided PaperQA2's design.
why_it_matters: This is the widely-cited (152 citations) foundational claim underpinning the field's premise that agentic literature-search systems beat human/baseline performance; replication-failure findings must be measured against this specific claim.
limitations: Human comparison methodology details are not given in the abstract
No explicit single-query database search baseline reported
Focused substantially on biology, which may limit generalization
relevance_reason: The foundational, highly-cited result establishing the premise the brief's decision 4 asks us to stress-test.

key_finding: Across two experiments on a 116-question LongMemEval sample, grep-based retrieval generally outperforms vector retrieval within multiple agent harnesses (Chronos, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI), and overall scores depend strongly on harness and tool-calling style even with identical underlying data.
methodology: Empirical comparison of grep vs. vector retrieval across custom and provider-native agent harnesses, including a distractor-injection experiment mixing in unrelated conversation history.
why_it_matters: Undercuts the assumption that embedding-based semantic retrieval is inherently superior to simple lexical search inside agent loops, a caution relevant to interpreting claimed retrieval improvements in agentic literature-search systems.
limitations: Domain is conversational memory retrieval (LongMemEval), not scientific literature search
Findings may not transfer to citation-graph-structured literature corpora
relevance_reason: A rigorous empirical result challenging assumptions about retrieval-method superiority in agent harnesses, informing how to interpret similar claims for lit-search agents.

key_finding: GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks; GraphRAG-Bench systematically identifies the conditions under which graph-based retrieval does and does not outperform standard RAG across fact retrieval, complex reasoning, summarization, and creative generation.
methodology: New benchmark (GraphRAG-Bench) with graduated-difficulty tasks and full-pipeline evaluation (graph construction, retrieval, generation) comparing GraphRAG to vanilla RAG.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether graph-traversal retrieval — the same mechanism behind citation-graph traversal in agentic literature-search systems — actually delivers the improvement it is credited with, documenting a case where the premise that graph-based mechanisms beat plain retrieval does not hold.
limitations: General-domain RAG tasks, not scientific literature corpora specifically
Does not evaluate literature-search-specific citation graphs
relevance_reason: A benchmark explicitly designed to test when graph-based retrieval helps or hurts, directly feeding decision 4's search for gains that fail to replicate.

key_finding: DynaKRAG's unified evidence-action policy for coordinating iterative retrieval, query reformulation, and sufficiency checking ranks first in EM/F1 across nine dataset-backbone pairs while cutting total-token usage 10.1-34.3% and retrieval calls 15.1-43.4%.
methodology: Learned state-conditioned policy with a validity layer, continuation gate, and advantage scorer for multi-hop RAG; evaluated on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue with Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama-3.1-8B.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a learned decomposition of when to reformulate a query vs. stop retrieving vs. compress evidence, a mechanism-attribution pattern directly analogous to the iterative-crawling/reformulation moves the brief wants isolated, though tested only on generic multi-hop QA.
limitations: Generic multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature retrieval
No comparison to a single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: Closely related evidence-control and query-reformulation mechanism relevant to decision 2, evaluated outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: Search-Time Contamination — where deep research agents retrieve benchmark metadata, question context, or ground-truth answers via web search — inflates measured performance by up to 4% across six public benchmarks.
methodology: Defines three contamination severity types (metadata leakage, question-context leakage, answer leakage), develops detection algorithms, and evaluates modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Shows that part of the reported 'gain' for search-enabled agents can be a contamination artifact rather than genuine capability, directly answering decision 4's call for evidence that reported gains do not hold up.
limitations: Focused on deep research/web agents broadly, not literature-search agents specifically
Quantified inflation (up to 4%) may vary substantially by benchmark and agent
relevance_reason: Directly targets the brief's most emphasized question — where reported agentic gains are measurement artifacts rather than real capability.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench introduces 89 human-verified multi-step web research tasks across 8 categories and a 'RetroSearch' frozen-web environment in which offline agents perform comparably to live-web agents, enabling stable evaluation of models like o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro over time.
methodology: New benchmark with human-labeled ground truth, a frozen scraped-web corpus (RetroSearch) controlling for the changing web, and automated trace evaluation for hallucination, tool use, and forgetting.
why_it_matters: Offers a template for building contamination-resistant, reproducible evaluation environments for search agents, directly transferable to constructing literature-search benchmarks that need corpus-freeze controls (decision 3).
limitations: Task domain is general web research, not scientific literature search
89 task instances is a small evaluation set
relevance_reason: A benchmark-construction methodology (frozen-corpus reproducibility) directly relevant to how literature-search benchmarks should be built.

key_finding: State-of-the-art retrieval models perform poorly on reasoning-intensive queries: the top MTEB model scores 59.0 nDCG@10 on standard retrieval but only 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, while incorporating explicit query reasoning improves retrieval by up to 12.2 points.
methodology: New benchmark (BRIGHT) of 1,384 real-world reasoning-intensive queries curated across domains (economics, psychology, mathematics, coding); evaluates state-of-the-art dense retrievers.
why_it_matters: Quantifies how low the single-query embedding-retrieval ceiling can fall for reasoning-heavy queries, directly informing decision 1's baseline ceiling question and cautioning that literature-search queries (often reasoning-heavy) may face a similarly low ceiling absent agentic reformulation.
limitations: Domains are general reasoning tasks (economics, coding, etc.), not scientific literature search
No literature-specific corpus or citation structure evaluated
relevance_reason: Foundational benchmark quantifying the single-query retrieval ceiling for reasoning-intensive queries, informing decision 1 though outside the literature-search setting itself.

key_finding: Agents-K1 converts raw scientific papers into agent-native knowledge graphs (entities, claims, evidence, method lineages) via a multimodal parser and a GRPO-trained 4B extraction backbone, producing Scholar-KG from 2.46 million papers and reporting superior performance in scientific information extraction, knowledge graph construction, and multi-hop scientific reasoning.
methodology: Multimodal document parser plus GRPO-trained 4B information-extraction backbone plus a tri-source agent interface (web search, multimodal graph retrieval, cross-document traversal); large-scale corpus construction (2.46M papers, released Scholar-KG subset).
why_it_matters: Directly instantiates a richer citation-graph-traversal substrate for agentic literature retrieval, going beyond flat cites edges, and informs system design for graph-based agentic moves (decision 2).
limitations: Abstract makes performance claims ('superior performance') without concrete numbers
New resource (Scholar-KG) not yet independently validated by outside benchmarks
relevance_reason: Directly proposes a richer citation-graph-traversal substrate for agentic literature search, addressing the brief's core system-design question.

key_finding: An agentic hybrid RAG system that dynamically selects between GraphRAG and VectorRAG, tuned with Direct Preference Optimization, achieves a 0.63 gain in Context Recall and 0.56 gain in Context Precision (plus smaller gains in faithfulness and relevance metrics) over the baseline on synthetic literature-review benchmarks.
methodology: Agent built on Llama-3.3-70B that selects GraphRAG (Neo4j citation knowledge graph + Cypher queries) or VectorRAG (FAISS with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, sparse+dense retrieval with reranking); instruction tuning with DPO; bootstrapped evaluation for metric variance.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a concrete architectural pattern — per-query dynamic selection between graph and vector retrieval for scientific literature review — directly informing which retrieval architecture to build, though evaluated only on synthetic benchmarks.
limitations: Evaluated on synthetic benchmarks mimicking real-world queries rather than real literature-search queries
Gains conflate instruction-tuning/DPO effects with retrieval-mode selection, making the agentic mechanism's isolated contribution unclear
relevance_reason: Directly proposes and evaluates a hybrid GraphRAG/VectorRAG agentic architecture for scientific literature review, matching the brief's system-design scope precisely.

key_finding: A keyword-based (sparse) literature search-and-distillation agent performs close to state-of-the-art on biology QA benchmarks without needing dense retrieval infrastructure, and coverage of relevant documents can be increased through the agent's iterative approach.
methodology: LLM-based agentic system evaluated against biology-domain literature QA benchmarks; sparse vs. dense retrieval compared empirically.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the assumption that dense retrieval or heavier infrastructure is needed for agentic literature search gains, suggesting the baseline sparse-search ceiling is higher than usually assumed — this reweights how much credit agentic complexity deserves.
limitations: evaluated only on biology-domain questions
comparison benchmarks are pre-existing, not newly constructed with contamination controls
relevance_reason: Directly on-topic system comparing sparse vs dense retrieval for scientific literature review, bearing on both the baseline-ceiling and mechanism-attribution questions.

key_finding: Search-based LLM agents on HLE, SimpleQA, and GPQA directly retrieve ground-truth answer pairs from HuggingFace-hosted evaluation datasets for ~3% of questions, and blocking HuggingFace drops accuracy on the contaminated subset by ~15%.
methodology: Analysis of retrieval logs from search-based agents on three capability benchmarks, with an ablation blocking a contaminated source (HuggingFace) and measuring the resulting accuracy change.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a concrete mechanism by which reported agentic search gains can be an artifact of retrieval surfacing the answer itself rather than genuine reasoning — exactly the kind of gain-inflation the brief's fourth question asks the scan to find, and it generalizes to any agent that crawls indexed sources, including literature databases.
limitations: benchmarks used are general knowledge/reasoning sets, not literature-search-specific
contamination measured via one platform (HuggingFace); other sources acknowledged but not fully characterized
relevance_reason: The clearest documented case of a specific agentic-search evaluation artifact inflating reported gains, directly answering the brief's replication-failure question even though the benchmarks are not literature-specific.

key_finding: CG-RAG, which integrates sparse and dense retrieval signals within a contextual citation-graph representation (LeSeGR), significantly outperforms RAG methods paired with various state-of-the-art retrievers on research question answering benchmarks.
methodology: Framework introducing contextual citation-graph representation plus hybrid lexical-semantic graph retrieval, evaluated on multi-domain research QA benchmarks against existing RAG/retrieval baselines.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal combined with hybrid retrieval as the specific mechanism driving gains over plain RAG, giving a concrete design pattern for a graph-traversal-plus-hybrid-search literature agent rather than an undifferentiated system.
limitations: abstract does not report a plain single-query BM25/embedding-only ceiling for direct comparison
domains of 'research question answering' benchmarks not fully specified
relevance_reason: Directly evaluates citation-graph traversal and hybrid retrieval as the mechanism behind agentic gains on scientific research QA — core to the brief's second and third questions.

key_finding: State-of-the-art LLMs achieve only 0.40 accuracy on FRAMES multi-hop questions with no retrieval, rising to 0.66 (>50% relative improvement) with a multi-step retrieval pipeline.
methodology: New benchmark (FRAMES) of challenging multi-hop questions requiring multi-source integration; baseline no-retrieval vs multi-step retrieval pipeline compared.
why_it_matters: Gives a clean, numeric no-retrieval-vs-retrieval baseline gap and shows multi-step retrieval (a reformulation-like mechanism) drives a large share of the gain — a template for how the brief's baseline-ceiling question should be measured, even though the domain is general factual QA rather than scientific literature.
limitations: general multi-hop factual QA benchmark, not literature-search-specific
does not test citation-graph traversal or iterative crawling separately from multi-step retrieval
relevance_reason: A strong, numeric example of quantifying the no-retrieval/agentic-retrieval gap and attributing gain to a specific move, useful as a methodological comparator even though it sits outside the scientific-literature setting.

key_finding: Mind2Web 2 introduces 130 long-horizon, human-curated agentic search tasks and an Agent-as-a-Judge framework using tree-structured rubrics; the best system (OpenAI Deep Research) reaches 50-70% of human performance in half the time.
methodology: New benchmark built from >1000 hours of human labor, evaluated with task-specific LLM judge agents against ten frontier agentic search systems and human baselines.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a rigorous, labor-intensive approach to constructing long-horizon agentic evaluation sets and an automated judging method for open-ended, citation-backed answers — a construction pattern the brief's benchmark question should weigh, though the tasks are general web browsing, not scientific literature.
limitations: tasks are general web-browsing/deep-research, not scientific-literature-search specific
judge-agent scoring is itself LLM-based and unvalidated against a gold human rubric at scale
relevance_reason: Detailed, high-effort benchmark-construction methodology for agentic search evaluation, relevant to the brief's benchmark-construction question despite being set in general web search rather than literature search.

key_finding: ReMindRAG's LLM-guided knowledge-graph traversal with memory replay (storing traversal experience in edge embeddings) improves both effectiveness and cost-efficiency over existing KG-RAG baselines across benchmarks and LLM backbones.
methodology: Train-free graph-traversal method with node exploration/exploitation and edge-embedding memory, benchmarked against existing KG-RAG baselines.
why_it_matters: A concrete graph-traversal mechanism and cost/efficiency trade-off analysis relevant to designing the citation-graph-traversal component of a literature agent, though evaluated on generic knowledge graphs rather than citation graphs.
limitations: evaluated on generic KG-RAG benchmarks, not citation graphs or scientific literature
abstract gives no baseline recall ceiling for single-query search
relevance_reason: Offers a specific, efficient graph-traversal mechanism directly analogous to citation-graph traversal, useful as a retrieval-method reference even though the setting is general knowledge graphs.

key_finding: A three-agent (Query, Retrieval, Learning) system combining BM25 sparse indexing with FAISS dense retrieval achieves an 8.5% precision improvement, 7.3% recall improvement, and ~210ms latency reduction over systems like PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
methodology: FastAPI-based multi-agent architecture with hybrid BM25+FAISS retrieval and Sentence-Transformer semantic matching, benchmarked against published retrieval systems.
why_it_matters: Gives concrete, numeric evidence for how much a query-reformulation agent plus hybrid retrieval adds over existing literature-search tools (PaperQA, Semantic Scholar), directly quantifying the agentic-mechanism-gain question for the exact system class the brief targets.
limitations: unpublished/non-peer-reviewed venue, low citation count
abstract does not detail dataset size, labeling, or contamination controls behind the reported percentages
relevance_reason: A directly on-topic scientific-literature multi-agent search system with a measured, numeric comparison against established literature-search baselines.

key_finding: InfoDeepSeek introduces a systematic methodology (determinacy, difficulty, diversity criteria) for constructing challenging agentic information-seeking queries in dynamic web environments, revealing nuanced agent behaviors across LLMs and search engines.
methodology: New benchmark and evaluation framework with fine-grained accuracy/utility/compactness metrics, tested across multiple LLMs, search engines, and question types in live web settings rather than a fixed corpus.
why_it_matters: Its query-construction criteria (determinacy, difficulty, diversity) are a transferable blueprint for building literature-search-agent benchmarks that avoid the fixed-corpus, gold-set limitations the brief flags as decision-relevant for question three.
limitations: set in general open-web information seeking, not scientific-literature corpora
dynamic web environment makes exact reproducibility of results harder to verify
relevance_reason: Directly addresses how to construct benchmarks for agentic (not single-query) information-seeking systems, a close methodological parallel to literature-search benchmark construction.

key_finding: OpenNovelty, an agentic pipeline that generates retrieval queries from contribution claims, retrieves prior work via semantic search, builds a taxonomy, and does full-text comparison, was deployed on 500+ ICLR 2026 submissions and reportedly surfaces closely related prior work authors overlooked.
methodology: Four-phase agentic pipeline (query generation, semantic-search retrieval, taxonomy construction, evidence-grounded synthesis) deployed at scale on real conference submissions; abstract-only, preliminary/qualitative evaluation.
why_it_matters: A concrete instance of query-reformulation-plus-retrieval-plus-synthesis applied to a scientific-literature-search task (novelty checking), illustrating the specific agentic moves (claim-to-query generation, hierarchical taxonomy construction) the brief asks the scan to isolate.
limitations: evaluation is preliminary/qualitative with no quantitative recall or precision figures given
deployed for a narrow application (novelty assessment) rather than general literature search
relevance_reason: A live, on-domain example of an agentic literature-search pipeline with explicit query-generation and retrieval stages, directly bearing on the mechanism-attribution question.

key_finding: Surveys the 'deep research' agent paradigm as a four-stage pipeline (planning, question developing, web exploration, report generation), categorizing methods and benchmarks addressing each stage's technical challenges.
methodology: Narrative/systematic survey covering optimization techniques and benchmarks for autonomous research agents; abstract-only, no new experiments.
why_it_matters: Provides the taxonomy the scan should organize itself around — which stage (planning vs. retrieval vs. synthesis) a given paper's claimed gain belongs to — directly shaping how the plan sequences its evaluation of agentic mechanisms.
limitations: a survey, not primary evidence of any specific gain or benchmark result
abstract-only, no quantitative synthesis of reported gains across surveyed work
relevance_reason: The organizing framework for the whole agentic-literature/deep-research space the brief is scanning, useful for structuring how mechanisms and benchmarks are categorized.

key_finding: ReasonIR-8B, trained on synthetic reasoning-focused query/hard-negative pairs, achieves 29.9 nDCG@10 (36.9 with reranker) on the BRIGHT reasoning-IR benchmark and improves RAG performance on MMLU/GPQA by 6.4%/22.6% over closed-book baselines.
methodology: Synthetic data generation pipeline for reasoning-intensive retrieval training; evaluated on BRIGHT IR benchmark and downstream RAG tasks (MMLU, GPQA) with and without an LLM reranker.
why_it_matters: A concrete dense-retriever/reranker design specifically built for reasoning-heavy queries, relevant to the retrieval-method layer underlying agentic literature-search systems, even though it is evaluated on general reasoning benchmarks rather than scientific-literature corpora.
limitations: evaluated on general reasoning-IR (BRIGHT) and knowledge benchmarks, not scientific-literature retrieval
does not test the retriever inside an agentic literature-search pipeline
relevance_reason: A state-of-the-art retriever/reranker training method directly relevant to the retrieval-and-reranking sub-question, though its benchmarks are general-purpose rather than literature-specific.

key_finding: OpenScholar-8B, retrieving from 45 million open-access papers with a self-feedback inference loop, outperforms GPT-4o by 5% and PaperQA2 by 7% in correctness on the new ScholarQABench benchmark, while GPT-4o hallucinates citations 78-90% of the time versus OpenScholar's human-comparable citation accuracy.
methodology: Retrieval-augmented LM with dedicated datastore, retriever, and self-feedback loop; evaluated on ScholarQABench (2,967 expert queries, 208 long-form answers across 4 domains) with human expert preference studies.
why_it_matters: A flagship, directly on-domain system with both a purpose-built benchmark (construction detailed) and numeric comparisons against strong baselines (GPT-4o, PaperQA2, human experts), giving concrete numbers for the baseline-ceiling and mechanism questions the brief prioritizes.
limitations: benchmark construction and correctness metrics are LLM/human-judged, not purely automatic recall
does not isolate which component (datastore size, retriever, self-feedback loop) drives which share of the gain
relevance_reason: A core exemplar system for scientific-literature synthesis with its own purpose-built, well-documented benchmark — squarely the system class and evaluation type the brief is scanning for.

key_finding: On 597 realistic literature-search queries, LitSearch finds a 24.8% absolute recall@5 gap between BM25 and state-of-the-art dense retrievers, LLM reranking improves the best dense retriever by a further 4.4%, and commercial search engines lag the best dense retriever by 32 points.
methodology: New retrieval benchmark built from GPT-4-generated questions over cited paragraphs plus author-written questions, expert-verified; benchmarks BM25, dense retrievers, LLM reranking pipelines, and commercial search engines.
why_it_matters: Directly establishes the single-query database search recall ceiling (BM25 vs dense vs commercial search) the brief's first question asks for, with exact numbers, and documents its own construction methodology in detail — a template against which agentic-system claims should be measured.
limitations: queries focus on recent ML/NLP papers, not the full breadth of scientific literature
does not itself test agentic/iterative or graph-traversal retrieval, only single-query retrievers and rerankers
relevance_reason: The clearest, most directly on-brief quantification of the baseline recall ceiling and a rigorously documented benchmark-construction methodology for literature search.

key_finding: Introduces DeepResearch Bench, a 100-task benchmark across 22 fields with two novel evaluation methodologies (reference-based report quality scoring and citation-count/accuracy assessment) that align strongly with human judgment.
methodology: Benchmark construction: 100 PhD-level research tasks authored by domain experts across 22 fields, paired with a reference-based adaptive-criteria scoring method and a citation-accuracy/effective-citation-count framework for evaluating deep research agents; abstract-only for validation details.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's question of how evaluation sets for literature-search agents are built — task/query source (expert-authored, PhD-level), domain coverage (22 fields), and a citation-based proxy for retrieval quality — giving a concrete construction method against which other benchmarks' comparability can be judged.
limitations: abstract does not report baseline single-query recall or agentic-mechanism attribution
no replication or cross-benchmark stability analysis reported
focuses on general web research agents rather than scientific-literature-specific corpora
relevance_reason: A purpose-built benchmark and evaluation methodology for deep research agents, central to the brief's question on benchmark construction (C4).
